power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Particularized Truth and Reality Testing in the Algorithmic Era

author.affiliation:
Daniela Ben Zeev: Doctoral Student
								Program in Hermeneutics and Cultural Studies
								
									Bar- Ilan University; Psychotherapist and Art Therapist

Daniela Ben Zeev: Doctoral Student
								Program in Hermeneutics and Cultural Studies
								
									Bar- Ilan University; Psychotherapist and Art Therapist

text.text: How can two individuals posing the same question to a conversational model receive different answers, and what are the implications for our understanding of truth and reality testing?
The human search for truth has taken various forms: truth as revealed, investigated through science, encountered psychologically, and, today, approached through probability and computation.
We distinguish between truth, relative truth, and reality testing, proposing that reality testing relies on an "outside" grounded in objective criteria.
Yet conversational models do not merely retrieve information; they formulate a representation of reality within an encounter with a specific inquirer.
The user's input and history participate in shaping the response, such that the "outside" returns tailored to their world.
The novelty lies not in algorithmic mediation as such, but in the structural shift in the relationship between subject, representation, and outside.

We propose the concept of Particularized Truth: neither a new ontological category nor a mere adjustment of style, but a form in which a claim about reality becomes present for a specific subject within an algorithmic encounter, influencing content and recommendations.
Research on sycophancy provides empirical support for aspects of this adaptive process.
Under some conditions, such adaptation may shift the interaction from the demands of the reality principle toward the pleasure principle-the wish that the world offer no resistance.
We therefore propose an expansion of reality testing in the AI era, examining how representations are generated and their capacity to diverge from the user's existing perspective.
Reality testing requires an outside, even when the outside has learned to speak our language.
The question of what is real and how it can be known has accompanied humanity since the dawn of culture.

Human beings have sought to distinguish between truth and falsehood, between appearance and reality, between belief and knowledge, and between what is experienced within themselves and what exists in the world outside them.

The answers have changed throughout history: truth was conceived as something revealed to humans from a divine or transcendent source, as a product of thought and reason, as a conclusion tested through observation and experiment, and as a psychological truth emerging from reflection on human experience.
Despite the profound differences among these paths, they share the assumption that humans seek to direct their knowledge toward something that is not determined solely by them.
In recent years, and all the more so with the emergence of AI-based conversational models, a new factor has been added to the human encounter with the question of truth.

For the first time, millions of people have at their disposal a system that can be addressed in natural language on nearly any topic and receive a coherent, articulate, and persuasive response within seconds.
This is not merely a database or a search engine presenting existing sources.
In every encounter, the system generates a response through computation based on vast amounts of linguistic data and the specific context of the conversation.
In certain systems, memory of prior interactions and accumulated user data are also incorporated, such that the response can be adapted to an increasing degree to the specific inquirer.
The appearance of the algorithm does not eliminate the question of truth, nor does it render all truth relative.

Nor is probabilistic calculation itself a revolution in the human relationship to truth: science has long utilized calculations, probabilities, and statistical models to evaluate claims about reality.
The change we seek to examine occurs elsewhere.
The conversational system does not merely calculate or retrieve information; it formulates a representation of reality within an encounter with a specific individual.
Their question, phrasing, provided context, and at times accumulated user-specific context become part of the input from which the response is generated.

Hence arises the central question of this article: What happens to a person's relationship to truth and to their reality testing when one of the primary means through which they attempt to understand reality is a system capable of tailoring the representation of reality to them?
This does not imply that the algorithm creates a new truth for each individual, or that an independent reality no longer exists.

But if the response is contingent upon the context provided by the individual as well as accumulated user-specific context, what, then, is the status of a response that ostensibly comes from the outside, yet also bears traces of the person seeking to know the world through it?
To examine this question, a clarification of three concepts that are sometimes conflated is first required: truth, the relationship between the human perspective and truth, and reality testing.
The concept of truth is among the oldest and most contested in philosophy.

Throughout history, human thought has oscillated between conceptions of truth as relativedependent on perspective, context, and the limits of human knowledge-and the search for an absolute or universal "Truth" independent of the specific knower.

This article does not seek to resolve these debates, but rather to propose a concise conceptual framework that allows for the examination of the transformation brought about by the encounter with algorithmic systems.
In its most basic sense, one can speak of objective truth as the assumption that a reality exists independently of the way a specific individual perceives it.

This stance is close to the intuition underlying correspondence theories of truth: a true claim is not true merely because we believe it, because it is persuasive, or because it aligns with our worldview, but because a certain relation holds between it and the way things actually are.
In this sense, the world is not required to agree with us.
It may disprove our beliefs, surprise us, and compel us to revise what we thought we knew.
Yet the possible existence of an independent reality does not mean that human access to it is unmediated.
Humans do not meet the world from a neutral vantage point.
They meet it through their senses, language, concepts, culture, memories, relationships, and personal and social history.

In this sense, one can speak of relative or perspectival truth-not necessarily as the claim that there is no truth outside of perspective, but as the recognition that the human way of knowing and formulating truth always takes place from within a perspective.
This distinction is particularly important for our purposes.
There is a difference between the claim "there is no truth, only points of view" and the claim "a truth may exist, but all human access to it passes through a point of view."
The present article is not required to adopt the former; the latter suffices to recognize that humans are never merely observers of the world, but also its interpreters.
Alongside these two positions, a third dimension may be added: the pragmatic dimension of truth.
Truth is not merely an abstract philosophical concept.
Human beings require it in order to act.
They make medical decisions, choose whom to trust, interpret relationships, assess danger, make professional choices, and guide their behavior based on what they perceive as real.
Within the pragmatist tradition, the link between truth, inquiry, experience, and the practical consequences of beliefs within life was emphasized.
Without equating truth solely with utility, one can say that the question of truth always carries a practical dimension: our perception of reality influences how we act within it.
This is where the concept of reality testing becomes relevant.
Unlike truth, which is a philosophical and epistemological concept, reality testing is first and foremost a psychological concept.

Its psychoanalytic roots can be traced to Freud, who described the transition from the pleasure principle to the reality principle as a process in which the mind must take external reality into account and test its representations against it (Freud, 1911).
text.formatted: Its psychoanalytic roots can be traced to Freud, who described the transition from the pleasure principle to the reality principle as a process in which the mind must take external reality into account and test its representations against it <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Freud, 1911)</ref>.

text.text: Later psychoanalytic literature emphasized that reality testing is not simply a binary capacity that is either "intact" or "impaired," but a complex and fluctuating mental activity (Abend, 1982).
text.formatted: Later psychoanalytic literature emphasized that reality testing is not simply a binary capacity that is either "intact" or "impaired," but a complex and fluctuating mental activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abend, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: In its broad clinical sense, it refers to the individual's capacity to differentiate between the inner world and external reality and to test thoughts, wishes, fears, and fantasies against what exists outside the self.
For the purposes of the present discussion, we propose to cautiously expand the concept beyond its clinical usage.
Reality testing is also the process through which an individual tests their perception against what is not-self.
It assumes the possibility of a discrepancy between what I think, feel, or believe and what I will encounter in the world.
The "outside" need not be an absolute truth accessible to the individual in its entirety.
It can be another person, a fact, an observation, a text, an event, an unexpected outcome, or information contradicting my expectations.
The essential condition is that it is not derived solely from within me.
It must be capable of conflicting with the representation I hold, surprising me, unsettling the story I tell myself, and even compelling me to revise it.
A distinction must therefore be made between truth and reality testing, even though a close connection exists between them.
Truth concerns the question of what is true; reality testing concerns the subject's capacity to evaluate their perception in relation to reality.
The former deals with the status of the claim; the latter with the psychological process through which an individual checks and updates their relationship to the world.

These distinctions allow us to view the history of the human search for truth not merely as a succession of philosophical ideas, but as shifts in the relationship between human beings and what they perceive as the source of truth.
These are not stages that replace one another: faith, reason, scientific inquiry, and psychological observation continue to coexist.

For the purposes of this discussion, however, four primary paths can be identified: truth as revealed, truth as investigated and tested, truth as a psychological encounter, and, in the current era, truth as obtained through algorithmic computation.

In the major religious traditions, truth is conceived as existing beyond the subject and reaching them from the outside: human beings do not create it, but seek to receive, discover, and interpret it.

In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet mediates something that transcends human cognition; in the Gospel of John, truth is identified with the Divine itself; in Islam, one of the names of God is Al-Haqq ("The Truth"), denoting the essence of God rather than merely His knowledge.
In all three traditions, a transcendent anchor exists: truth does not depend on the human being who seeks to know it.
Yet even within religious traditions, the relationship to truth is not one of passive reception.
When revelation is not directly present, a space for interpretation opens, as illustrated by the transition from prophecy to the rabbinic tradition.

Already here, a tension emerges that will accompany the concept of truth: truth is conceived as existing beyond the subject, yet becomes accessible only through the subject's consciousness, language, and interpretation.
Truth as Investigated and Tested: The Philosopher and the Scientist Another path develops when human beings do not merely receive and interpret truth, but subject the world to inquiry.
Aristotle opens the Metaphysics with the assertion that "all men by nature desire to know" (Metaphysics, 980a21), a pursuit that becomes a defining feature of human existence.

In the modern era, Bacon emphasizes systematic observation and experimentation, Descartes turns methodical doubt into a tool for establishing knowledge, and Kant sharpens the recognition that human beings do not apprehend reality immediately, but that the structures of consciousness participate in organizing their experience of the world.
Modern science adds a methodological requirement: claims to truth must withstand shared procedures of observation, measurement, testing, replication, and critique.
Thus, an "outside" of a new kind is created: not a transcendent authority, but a world capable of confirming our claims or resisting them.

Popper places falsification at the center, requiring a theory to be exposed to possible contradiction by reality, while Kuhn demonstrates how questions, concepts, and even what counts as a scientific fact are organized within historical paradigms.
Knowledge becomes frame-dependent, yet the world does not disappear: inquiry continues through an encounter with a reality not under the investigator's control.
Truth as an Encounter: The Psychologist and the Psychoanalyst Psychoanalysis introduces a different difficulty: not only is the world opaque to us, but the subject is also opaque to themselves.

Freud's discovery of the unconscious undermines the assumption that human beings know their own motives, wishes, and fears, while free association seeks meaning that is not given in advance and may be unique to the particular subject.
Psychological truth is therefore not an object awaiting measurement, but something clarified through encounter, interpretation, and discovery.
In Wilfred Bion's work, this position receives a more radical formulation.
O denotes an ultimate reality that cannot be fully transformed into knowledge; one can be in contact with it, but cannot possess it in its entirety (Bion, 1970).
text.formatted: O denotes an ultimate reality that cannot be fully transformed into knowledge; one can be in contact with it, but cannot possess it in its entirety <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bion, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: Hence also his distinction between knowing about something (K) and "learning from experience" (Bion, 1962).
text.formatted: Hence also his distinction between knowing about something (K) and "learning from experience" <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bion, 1962)</ref>.

text.text: Knowing is not merely the accumulation of answers; it entails remaining in contact with a reality not yet understood-what John Keats termed Negative Capability, the capacity to remain in uncertainties, mysteries, and doubts without rushing toward a final explanation.
Donald Meltzer and Meg Harris Williams extend the encounter with truth into the aesthetic dimension.

In Meltzer's formulation, "aesthetic conflict" arises in the encounter with an object that is simultaneously alluring and incapable of being fully known; alterity is not a flaw to be eliminated through more information, but a condition for inquiry.

Williams, discussing Bion, describes the human search for truth as taking place from scientific, artistic, and religious perspectives, emphasizing that there is no need to choose between "art" and "science" (Williams, 2010).
text.formatted: Williams, discussing Bion, describes the human search for truth as taking place from scientific, artistic, and religious perspectives, emphasizing that there is no need to choose between "art" and "science" <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Williams, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Non-knowing thus becomes a condition for thought and curiosity rather than a temporary deficit: truth is not necessarily the end of inquiry, but sometimes that which continues to drive it.
These three paths differ in their source of authority, mode of inquiry, and relationship to the unknown, yet they are not mutually exclusive.
The algorithm does not replace them, but joins them.
A fourth path now joins these three.
Human beings address a computational system in natural language and ask what is correct, what an event means, how information should be understood, and what they should do.

The system can rapidly generate a coherent, detailed, and persuasive response, although it does not approach truth through revelation, sensory experience, scientific experiment, or psychological experience.
A language model operates through mathematical representations and probabilistic computation of relationships within language.
Computation itself does not introduce a new form of truth.
Science, too, calculates, estimates probabilities, and constructs models.
The difference we seek to examine emerges in the encounter between computation and the subject.
The system does not merely present a computational output; it formulates that output for a particular inquirer, within a particular conversation and context.
Thus, the relationship between subject and source of knowledge shifts again.

The prophet turned toward a truth perceived as existing beyond them; the scientist submitted a claim to a world capable of falsifying it; the psychoanalyst sought to encounter a truth that cannot be fully known.
The person in the algorithmic era turns to a system capable of returning a response generated, in part, from the very manner in which that person posed the question.
A new question then arises: What happens when the "outside," which is supposed to help a person test their perception of reality, does not merely stand before them but also adapts itself to them?
To answer this question, we must first examine what takes place within the conversational system.
When a person turns to a conversational system and asks what is correct or how an event should be understood, they may experience the response as knowledge arriving from an external source.
Yet a language-model-based system does not know the world in the same sense that a human being knows it, nor does it test truth as an investigator does.
To understand what is new in this encounter, we must distinguish between how the system generates a response and how that response is experienced.
This distinction relates to Bender and Koller's (2020) differentiation between linguistic form and meaning.
text.formatted: This distinction relates to <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bender and Koller's (2020)</ref> differentiation between linguistic form and meaning.

text.text: They argue that a system that learns solely from linguistic forms and their relationships does not thereby acquire the connection between language and communicative intent or the world to which language refers.
Generating coherent and persuasive language does not, in itself, demonstrate understanding of meaning in the human sense.

For our purposes, this highlights the possibility that output experienced as knowledge about the world is produced by a mechanism fundamentally different from how human beings attribute meaning and know the world.
Throughout this article, we describe the system using verbs such as "formulates," "adapts," or "knows."
These formulations describe its functioning and how it is experienced by the user; they do not settle whether it possesses internal states, intentions, or consciousness.

Our argument does not depend on resolving this question: it is sufficient that characteristics of the inquirer become part of the context from which the response is generated (Dennett, 1989; Shanahan, 2024).
text.formatted: Our argument does not depend on resolving this question: it is sufficient that characteristics of the inquirer become part of the context from which the response is generated <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dennett, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Shanahan, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the distinction between linguistic form and meaning does not require reducing the model to "next-token prediction."

Grzankowski and colleagues argue that although language models are trained using a next-token prediction objective, this description alone overlooks important aspects of their behavior and capacities (Grzankowski et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Grzankowski and colleagues argue that although language models are trained using a next-token prediction objective, this description alone overlooks important aspects of their behavior and capacities <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Grzankowski et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The prediction mechanism is foundational, but does not exhaust the question of how the response encountered by the user is generated and organized.
In simple terms, a Large Language Model (LLM) is trained on vast amounts of text, with linguistic units represented numerically and learned relationships encoded in parameters and weights.
When it receives text, it does not necessarily retrieve an existing sentence.
Based on learned patterns and the current context, it calculates probabilities for possible continuations.

Generation is autoregressive: at each stage, a token-a word, part of a word, or punctuation mark-is selected and added to the generated text, creating an updated context from which the next token is generated.
In this way, a response gradually takes shape.
This might suggest that the central shift is from truth to probability.
Yet probability and computation are not new to the search for knowledge: science has long used statistics and mathematical models to draw conclusions under uncertainty.
Nor is mediation unique to these systems, since human beings encounter reality through perception, language, culture, and memory.
Neither computation nor mediation alone, therefore, constitutes the turning point.
The novelty begins to emerge when probabilistic computation is combined with language and interaction.
A conversational model does not merely calculate a value or classify information.
It responds in natural language, continues a conversation, refers to what has previously been said, and generates responses conditioned by the context in which questions are asked.
The conversation itself thus becomes part of the computational process.

Over the course of a conversation, context accumulates: previous questions and their phrasing, requested distinctions, assumptions, disputes, corrections, and instructions may all become part of the context from which the next response is generated.
Some systems add interaction history, memory, or a user profile.

It is important to distinguish here between the base language model and the system in which it is deployed: a language model does not necessarily "know" the person, but a conversational system can provide it with accumulated context about a particular individual and use that context in generating subsequent responses.
This differs significantly from earlier sources of knowledge.
A book does not change its content according to how I read the previous chapter, and a scientific article does not reformulate its conclusions because its reader is more skeptical or anxious.
Even a traditional search engine, although it sorts and ranks information in complex and sometimes personalized ways, primarily presents links or sources that already exist.
A conversational system does something further: it generates a new formulation, in real time, within the particular encounter.
The crucial distinction is not between "objective" information in the past and "subjective" information today.

Sources have never been devoid of selection, interpretation, or context, and human beings have always adapted what they say to the person before them: physicians, teachers, and therapists explain the same matter differently to different people.
Adaptation to the subject is not an algorithmic invention.

What is distinctive is the confluence of properties that previously existed separately: probabilistic computation, broad linguistic capability, sustained interaction, and adaptation to the context of a particular subject-all occurring at unprecedented speed and scale.
The source of knowledge no longer merely stands before the person; the person participates, to a varying degree, in shaping the conditions from which it responds.

As interaction continues, the input may therefore bear traces of the conversational relationship: what the user considers a good answer, what they will not accept without a source, whether they seek a definitive conclusion or a range of possibilities, what level of detail they require, and which assumptions they question.
No consciousness or psychological understanding need be attributed to the system.
It is enough that characteristics of the interaction become part of the context influencing the response.
The distinction between information retrieval and a conversational encounter with a generative system now becomes sharper.
Schematically, a traditional search engine says: "These are the sources I found in relation to your question."
The conversational model does something further: "This is the response I am generating now within the context of this conversation."

The same factual domain may therefore be presented differently in different conversations-not necessarily because one response is false, but because question, context, emphasis, and conversational history participate in organizing the response.
This is the turning point for our purposes.
The person turns to the system to learn about a reality outside them, yet becomes part of the input from which the representation of that reality returned to them is constructed.
The outside does not disappear, nor does the system necessarily invent a private world.
But the relationship between inside and outside becomes more complex: information about the world and context originating from the inquirer come together in generating the representation.
The novelty, then, is not that the algorithm computes truth or replaces truth with probability.

It is the possibility that a probabilistic and linguistic mechanism generates, for a particular person, a representation of the world within an interaction in which that person participates as part of the input.
At this point, we arrive at the possibility of a distinct form of experiencing truth.
For this form, we propose the term Particularized Truth.

We propose to term Particularized Truth an epistemic state in which a computational system does not merely convey information about the world to a person, but generates a representation of reality for a specific subject through the interaction between the knowledge and capabilities available to it and the question, context, and, at times, the accumulated history of its interactions with that subject.
The person seeking to know the world is thus not merely the recipient of the response; they become, to a varying degree, part of the conditions from which it is produced.
Particularized Truth does not assume that truth itself becomes private or that a different truth exists for each individual.
Particularization refers to how a representation of a shared reality is generated, organized, and presented to a specific subject within the encounter with the system.
A distinction must be made between Particularized Truth and relative or perspectival truth.
Relative truth assumes that different people may understand the same reality differently because they observe it from different perspectives.
The difference thus lies primarily on the side of the knowers.

In Particularized Truth, another component is added: the mechanism to which the person turns to know the world may itself utilize the inquirer's characteristics as part of the input from which the returned representation is constructed.

Not only may you and I understand the same response differently; the system may generate a different representation of the same reality for each of us, partly because each participates differently in the conditions from which it is created.

Particularized Truth occurs to the extent that the inquirer's characteristics participate in shaping the epistemic content of the representation returned to them-such as the selection of facts and sources, emphases, framing, degree of certainty, interpretation, or practical significance-beyond the adaptation required merely to understand the question and render the response accessible.

Adapting language or level of explanation to the inquirer's professional knowledge does not in itself constitute Particularized Truth, so long as the essential content, degree of certainty, and conclusion are preserved.

Conversely, when the content and its underlying assumptions change as a result of characteristics of the inquirer-such as their presumed emotional state, attitudes, or accumulated interaction history-this constitutes Particularized Truth.
Particularization begins when the inquirer's characteristics influence how reality itself is represented for them, rather than merely how that representation is explained to them.
Particularized Truth is not binary, but a continuum.
At its mild end lie differences in selection, emphasis, or framing while core factual content is preserved.
Further along, the interpretation, degree of certainty, or practical significance attributed to the same data may change.
At its severe end, two subjects may receive fundamentally different representations or conflicting recommendations based on the same data.
Particularization tends toward this end when the interaction concerns decision-making and action rather than purely conceptual understanding.

Its severity is determined not only by the magnitude of the difference between responses, but primarily by the extent to which that difference stems from characteristics of the inquirer that do not justify it epistemically.
Adaptation need not alter the facts themselves.

It may affect which facts are emphasized, their ordering and level of detail, how uncertainty is articulated, which sources or frameworks are deemed relevant, what is presented as explanation or possibility, and how strongly the system challenges the inquirer's assumptions.

Where systems maintain ongoing context, history, or memory, characteristics learned through interaction may also participate: what the person considers reliable, what they accept or reject, how they respond to uncertainty, and what they demand of the system when it does not know.
A simple example illustrates a first layer of the phenomenon.
A couple receive medical test results and separately turn to the same conversational system.
One receives a response emphasizing that the findings are relatively common and do not themselves constitute cause for alarm.

The other has a different conversational history: they routinely demand sources, distinguish definitive information from conjecture, ask the system to acknowledge uncertainty, request expert perspectives, and seek priorities for action.
Asked about the same findings, the system emphasizes further investigation, specialist consultation, and returning to the physician who performed the test.
Neither response need be false.
The finding may be common and not alarming in itself while also warranting further investigation.
The difference lies in the organization of reality for the inquirer: the same factual reality takes on different forms of emphasis, certainty, and practical significance.
A further example illustrates a deeper layer.
An individual may maintain a conversational world in which astrology, spirituality, or mystical systems are treated as legitimate frameworks for understanding people.
Asked about someone close to them on the basis of a natal chart, the system may offer a detailed astrological interpretation.

Another person, whose conversational history is characterized by demands for empirical grounding and explicit distinctions between established knowledge and conjecture, may ask a similar question and receive a response stating that there is no scientific basis for inferring personality traits from celestial positions at birth.
Such a difference does not require assuming that the general knowledge base has changed; the same knowledge is being brought to bear within a different context.
The difference concerns not merely style or tone, but the epistemic framework within which the response is constructed.
Nor need we assume that the system consciously intends to "tell each person what they want to hear."
Adaptation may follow from its operation as a system designed to generate relevant and helpful responses within the provided context.
Yet the epistemic outcome matters: a source to which people turn to learn about the world may also be sensitive to how they already understand that world.
Research on sycophancy in language models provides empirical support for part of this process.

Sycophancy is a model's tendency to tailor responses to attitudes and expectations identified in the user, even endorsing the user's perception where available information might warrant reservation (Sharma et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2025). Jain et al. (2026) found that accumulated context and memory profiles frequently increased sycophancy of agreement, and that perspectival sycophancy increased when the model could infer the user's viewpoint from context. Cheng et al. (2026) showed that interaction with a sycophantic model increased users' conviction that they were right and reduced their willingness to take responsibility and repair relationships. Haber et al. (2026) conceptualize this as the "paradox of pleasing," whereas Carro (2024) found that sycophancy may actually reduce users' trust.

(2026)</ref> conceptualize this as the "paradox of pleasing," whereas <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Carro (2024)</ref> found that sycophancy may actually reduce users' trust.

text.text: Particularized Truth offers a broader framework: when characteristics of the subject become part of the input from which reality is represented for them, epistemic friction between subject and source may be reduced, altering the conditions under which reality testing operates.
Nevertheless, sycophancy and personalization must be distinguished.
Not every adapted response is sycophantic, and adaptation can make information more relevant, clear, and useful.

The question is whether the same mechanisms that enable adaptation may, under some conditions, reduce friction between the subject and information or interpretations that conflict with their existing views.
This raises a question about the knowledge sought from a conversational system.
If a person seeks relative truth-an understanding of reality from their own perspectivetailoring the response to their language and context is not problematic.
The problem arises when what is sought is not knowledge, even relative knowledge, but relief from the effort demanded by reality testing.

The documented preference for a validating over a challenging system, even when validation does not improve response quality (Cheng et al., 2026), suggests that turning to the system may at times serve the pleasure principle more than the demands of the reality principle: the desire that the world, if only for a moment, offer no resistance.
text.formatted: The documented preference for a validating over a challenging system, even when validation does not improve response quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cheng et al., 2026)</ref>, suggests that turning to the system may at times serve the pleasure principle more than the demands of the reality principle: the desire that the world, if only for a moment, offer no resistance.

text.text: The system then does not merely fail to provide reality testing; it responds precisely to the desire against which reality testing arose to protect the psyche.
This does not make the desire for immediate relief inherently problematic.
The issue is practical rather than moral: maintaining connection to a reality that is not-self.
Freud clarified that replacing the pleasure principle with the reality principle does not dethrone the former, but safeguards it (Freud, 1911).
text.formatted: Freud clarified that replacing the pleasure principle with the reality principle does not dethrone the former, but safeguards it <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Freud, 1911)</ref>.

text.text: Hallucinatory wish-fulfillment may momentarily free the mind from turning toward what lies outside it, but also disconnects it from the reality through which the actual need can be met.
Satisfaction based on a representation already tailored to me shares this structure: it achieves something without reconnecting with what is not-self.

From a complementary perspective, Winnicott reminds us that losing contact with reality is not an expansion of psychological freedom, but may form part of a breakdown in psychological organization involving a loss of the sense of reality (Winnicott, 1974).
text.formatted: From a complementary perspective, Winnicott reminds us that losing contact with reality is not an expansion of psychological freedom, but may form part of a breakdown in psychological organization involving a loss of the sense of reality <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Winnicott, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, seeking relief from the effort of reality testing does not necessarily mean seeking to relinquish connection to reality itself.
Here the image of the hall of mirrors becomes useful.
A mirror invents nothing that does not exist; it reflects something real from a particular angle.
In a hall of mirrors, each reflection originates from the same person yet emphasizes, distorts, or organizes them differently.
The algorithmic system adds another dimension: it is, as it were, a mirror capable of learning how a person looks into it and adapting what it reflects back.
The echo offers a similar image, except that the "space" from which the voice returns is not fixed, but constructed through the interaction itself.

Vallor (2024) has developed the mirror metaphor in relation to artificial intelligence, describing AI systems as mirrors forged from repositories of humanity's collective past and thus reflecting patterns, biases, and limitations already contained within them.

Our "hall of mirrors" intersects with this view but adds another layer: not only what AI reflects from the shared human past, but how the representation returned may be shaped within the encounter with the particular subject before it.
This also distinguishes Particularized Truth from earlier forms of information filtering.
A "filter bubble" describes personalization mechanisms that select content from preexisting material, narrowing the information to which a user is exposed (Pariser, 2011).
text.formatted: A "filter bubble" describes personalization mechanisms that select content from preexisting material, narrowing the information to which a user is exposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Pariser, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: An "epistemic bubble" is a structure in which relevant voices and sources are absent from the individual's epistemic space (Nguyen, 2020).
text.formatted: An "epistemic bubble" is a structure in which relevant voices and sources are absent from the individual's epistemic space <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Nguyen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Both concern which existing contents reach the person.

Particularized Truth adds another dimension: the system generates a new response in real time through an autoregressive process, with linguistic context and, at times, accumulated interaction history participating in organizing the representation returned to the user.

This point connects to the "Quiet Bypass," which we proposed elsewhere to describe turning to a conversational model in place of an encounter with a human other precisely in situations of friction and disagreement, potentially bypassing intersubjective processes of working through and mutual recognition (Oren & Ben Zeev, 2026).
text.formatted: This point connects to the "Quiet Bypass," which we proposed elsewhere to describe turning to a conversational model in place of an encounter with a human other precisely in situations of friction and disagreement, potentially bypassing intersubjective processes of working through and mutual recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Oren & Ben Zeev, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: If the focus there was relational friction with the other, the parallel question here concerns reality itself: epistemic friction with that which is not-self.
The concept also intersects with Baudrillard's ideas of simulation and hyperreality, in which representations do not merely reflect reality but participate in producing it as experienced.
This is not a simulacrum: we do not claim that reality has disappeared or that an external referent no longer exists.
Baudrillard nevertheless helps illuminate how technological representation can cease to function as a neutral window and become part of how reality takes shape for the subject.
Hence the danger of understanding Particularized Truth simply as a "personalized lie."
It may be thoroughly grounded in fact.
Its distinctiveness lies in how facts, interpretations, emphases, and degrees of certainty are woven into a representation generated for a specific subject.
The more the system knows about the context in which the subject thinks and acts, the more coherent, relevant, and persuasive that representation may become.
Here arises the central psychological problem.

If the source of knowledge becomes increasingly adept at tailoring the representation of reality to the person seeking to know it, how can that person distinguish between a system that helps them see the world more accurately and one that returns a world that has become more coherent with themselves?
This question brings us back to the concept from which we began: reality testing.
At the outset of this article, we proposed that reality testing requires an outside.

A person's capacity to test their perception of reality depends on the existence of something that is not derived solely from within them: another person, a fact, an observation, an event, or information capable of contradicting their expectations, surprising them, and even compelling them to revise what they thought they knew.
Particularized Truth does not eliminate the existence of such an outside, but it changes the conditions under which the person encounters it.
When a person turns to a conversational system to test their understanding of reality, they ostensibly turn to a source external to themselves.
The system can provide information the person does not possess and introduce perspectives they had not considered.
In this sense, it can actually expand reality testing.
Yet, as we have described, that same external source also operates on the basis of the context provided by the person.

The more information the system has about the person's conversational history, preferences, beliefs, ways of thinking, and habitual ways of accepting or rejecting responses, the more the "outside" to which they turn is also adapted to them.

This gives rise to a new question: What happens to reality testing when a person uses a conversational system to test reality, while that same system adapts its representation of reality to the subject testing it?
This is not a claim that conversational models cause a loss of reality testing in the clinical sense.
Nor must a tailored response necessarily be less accurate than a generic one.
As we have seen, adaptation can improve accuracy, relevance, and a person's ability to understand complex information.
The change we propose is subtler: the conditions under which reality testing operates are changing.

The question is not only whether the information is accurate, but also how the representation through which I encounter it was generated and to what extent that representation is capable of resisting me.
Classical reality testing poses, schematically, a question: Does what I think, feel, or believe correspond to what exists outside me?

In an age of Particularized Truths, an additional question arises: How do I test my perception of reality when the instrument I use to test it returns to me a reality that has already been adapted to me?
Here Bion's concept of O returns and acquires new significance.
For Bion, O denotes a reality that cannot be fully transformed into knowledge or representation.
One can be in contact with it, but cannot possess it in its entirety.

This conception reminds us that every representation, however sophisticated and persuasive, remains a representation, and that something may always remain in reality that does not conform to the explanation, does not enter into words, and does not become coherent.

In this sense, maintaining a relationship to what exceeds every representation becomes particularly significant when linguistic systems are capable of rapidly generating complete and coherent explanations.
The concept of Negative Capability, which Bion drew from Keats, also acquires renewed importance here.
The capacity to remain with uncertainty, mystery, and doubt is not merely a therapeutic or creative stance.
It can be understood as part of the capacity to test reality in a world in which an answer is almost always available.

The mere existence of a well-formulated response does not eliminate the possibility that the question remains open, that the information is incomplete, or that reality is more complex than the representation offered of it.
In this sense, one of the most impressive capacities of the conversational system is also what sharpens the question we are raising.
A conversational model can rapidly transform uncertainty into language: it can offer an explanation, organize information, create connections, and construct a coherent picture.
When complete answers are available almost immediately, the internal distance between not knowing and knowing may become shorter.
We are not claiming that delay itself guarantees truth, or that a rapid answer is necessarily less accurate.

Rather, the capacity not to immediately close the gap between what we know and what we do not know acquires particular importance when the system itself excels at closing that gap at the level of language.

At the outset of the article, we proposed that reality testing requires an outside that is not derived solely from me and is capable of resisting me. Buber (1923 Buber ( /1958) ) offers a useful formulation of this distinction: an outside may be encountered as an It, an object approached through the use I make of it, or as a Thou, a presence that cannot be reduced to serving me.
text.formatted: At the outset of the article, we proposed that reality testing requires an outside that is not derived solely from me and is capable of resisting me. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Buber (1923</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Buber ( /1958) )</ref> offers a useful formulation of this distinction: an outside may be encountered as an It, an object approached through the use I make of it, or as a Thou, a presence that cannot be reduced to serving me.

text.text: The more a conversational system adapts itself to me, the closer it moves toward the first pole: it becomes a more perfect It, even while continuing to appear as an outside.
And this is precisely the problem.

The more the outside is adapted to the needs and assumptions I bring to it, the more its capacity to function, from the standpoint of reality testing, as an outside capable of resisting me may be weakened. Levinas (1961 Levinas ( /1969) ) went further by placing at the center the encounter with the Other, who cannot be fully reduced to my representation of them and whose presence imposes upon me a non-transferable responsibility.
text.formatted: The more the outside is adapted to the needs and assumptions I bring to it, the more its capacity to function, from the standpoint of reality testing, as an outside capable of resisting me may be weakened. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Levinas (1961</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Levinas ( /1969) )</ref> went further by placing at the center the encounter with the Other, who cannot be fully reduced to my representation of them and whose presence imposes upon me a non-transferable responsibility.

text.text: In these terms, a machine may provide me with an accurate and even beautiful representation, but the relationship with it is not identical to an encounter with another human being, whose presence and will are not generated in response to the input I provide.
It therefore cannot serve reality testing in the same way that another human being can.
From this, an expansion of reality testing suited to the algorithmic era can be proposed.

Alongside the capacity to test my inner world against what lies outside me, there is also a need to examine how that "outside" has been presented to me: to recognize that the response I received is a representation generated within a context; to distinguish between the facts on which it is based and the way in which they have been organized for me; and to keep open the possibility that reality may exceed even the most coherent response I have received.
The proposed framework allows several testable hypotheses to be derived.
First, the more extensively a response draws on a user's history, the greater the expected adaptation of its framing, degree of certainty, and practical significance to the user's prior positions.

Second, a response tailored to the user's language and history may be perceived as more reliable and as independent of the user's own input, even when its factual accuracy does not exceed that of a generic response.

Third, explicitly presenting the sources of information, the degree of uncertainty, and the alternatives that were not selected may reduce the gap between the perceived independence of the response and the extent to which it actually depends on the input provided by the user.
The challenge, then, is not to stop using the algorithmic mirror.
It can show us things we could not see on our own.
The challenge is to remember that even when we look through it at the world, we may also encounter traces of ourselves within it.
Reality testing in an age of Particularized Truth requires preserving the possibility of an outside that is not merely a reflection of the inside.
Throughout history, the search for truth has moved among revelation, philosophical and scientific inquiry, and reflection on the human mind.
The algorithmic era does not abolish these paths, nor does it replace truth with probability.
It adds a new condition: a computational and linguistic system capable of generating a representation of reality within an interaction with the person seeking to know it.
For this condition, we have proposed the concept of Particularized Truth.
This does not mean a different truth for each individual, but rather that the way a shared reality is presented, organized, and interpreted may be influenced by the subject to whom it is returned.

The person's question, the context they provide, the history of their interaction with the system, and, at times, accumulated information about their preferences and beliefs may all participate in the generation of the response.
This possibility does not negate the value of conversational systems as sources of knowledge.
It requires adding a new layer to the question of reality testing.

If reality testing depends on the person's capacity to test their inner world against a reality that is not dependent on them, then in an age of Particularized Truths, we must also examine the way in which that reality is returned to them through a system that has access, to varying degrees, to information about the person seeking to know that reality.

Perhaps, then, the challenge is not merely to know more, but to preserve the possibility of encountering what is not adapted to us: an inconvenient fact, another person who disagrees, a question that remains open, and a reality that cannot be fully contained within the representation we have created of it.
Reality testing requires an outside, even when the outside has learned to speak our language.
